sources.note: Orma phonology, not Waata. Section 8.3 'Tone in other Oromo languages' (printed p. 35, p. 36) quotes Heine 1981: 23 second-hand: tone 'does not seem to have any distinctive function in Waata'. Fn. 20: Tana River Waata and Orma consider their languages identical. Nothing on Waata stress placement; for Orma it reports the BTL 2005 view that 'Tone functions independently of stress' and that Oromo languages may be pitch accent.

sources.citation: Awadh, Omar Nafisa. 2022. Uchanganuzi wa makosa ya kimofofonolojia ya wanafunzi wa Kiwaaṱa wanapojifunza lugha ya Kiswahili [Analysis of the morphophonological errors of Kiwaata-speaking learners of Kiswahili]. Tasnifu ya shahada ya uzamili (MA thesis), Chuo Kikuu cha Pwani (Pwani University), Kilifi, March 2022. xv + 107 pp. (122 PDF pages).http://elibrary.pu.ac.ke/handle/123456789/1036.Waata phonology = sec. 4.2, printed pp. 39-70; prosody (kiimbo, mkazo) pp. 58-59; recommendation p. 98.

tone.quote: 4.2.2.4 Mkazo. Sifa hii hushughulikia jinsi watu wanavyotamka maneno kwa nguvu zaidi katika sehemu fulani. Mkazo unaweza kudhihirika katika sentensi au katika neno. Lugha ya Kiwaaṱa nayo hudhihirisha mkazo katika maneno mbalimbali kama vile: Ṱa’ṱa (Kaeni) ’Ṱaṱa (Jina la heshima la mwanamume) [p. 59] ... Vilevile, kutokana na utafiti uliofanywa, mtafiti anapendekeza yeyote yule atakayefanya utafiti wa Lugha hii ya Kiwaaṱa azigatie Fonolojia arudhi kama vile toni, shadda na mkazo na namna zinavyoathiri matumizi ya lugha ya Kiwaaṱa. [p. 98]
tone.locator: p. 59, sec. 4.2.2.4 'Mkazo'; p. 98, sec. 5.4 'Mapendekezo' (locators as given by S are correct; page numbers are printed at the head of each page)
tone.translation: 4.2.2.4 Stress. This feature concerns how people pronounce words with more force in a certain part. Stress can appear in the sentence or in the word. The Kiwaata language too shows stress in various words, for example: Ṱa’ṱa ('Sit down!', pl.) vs ’Ṱaṱa (a man's honorific name) [p. 59] ... Likewise, on the basis of the research done, the researcher recommends that anyone who studies this Kiwaata language should consider prosodic phonology such as tone, gemination and stress and how they affect the use of Kiwaata. [p. 98]
